title: Meshed attention kernel tracing — experiment log
content:
Purpose and context:
This note captures an experimental approach and intermediate findings from a targeted set of profiling runs aimed at surfacing interaction effects between FlashAttention, paged attention (flash-paged), and fused ops under mixed-sequence workloads. The goal is to understand transient regression modes that don't show up in long steady-state throughput curves but cause 95/99th latency spikes and occasional token jitter. We call the approach "meshed kernel tracing" because it combines: (1) fine-grained GPU timeline traces (ns resolution), (2) kernel-entry stack annotations from our runtime, (3) synthetic, controller-driven sequence mixes, and (4) a small perturbation matrix that flips fusion/quantization and prefetch knobs per-run.
High-level hypotheses:
1) Fusion toggles (fused ops enabled vs disabled) create multi-kernel handoffs that amplify small queueing jitter into measurable tail-latency events when the KV cache hitmix is >60% and sequence-length variance is high.
2) FlashPaged prefetch/backpressure interacts nonlinearly with FlashAttention's memory layout when row-block alignment crosses warp boundaries — causing intermittent register pressure and thread divergence.
3) Microburst arrival patterns (short trains of 8–32 requests) expose a scheduling gap in our batch coalescer that increases the probability of an unfused fallback path right at the microburst tail.
Experiment matrix (short):
- Workload mixes: 
  * A: uniform short (avg 32 tokens)
  * B: long-only (avg 1024 tokens)
  * C: bimodal mix (70% short 32, 30% long 1024)
  * D: entropy mix (sequence lengths sampled from heavy-tailed distribution; sigma large)
- KV cache hit ratios: 20%, 60%, 95%
- Fusion: on/off
- FlashPaged: enabled/disabled
- Quant: fp16, int8-qat
- Arrival: steady poisson vs microburst trains (burst length 16, 32)
- Replicates: 6 runs per cell; each run 120s with warmup 20s
Measurements collected:
- GPU timeline (ns) per-stream and per-kernel occupancy
- Kernel name, argument shape, chosen kernel variant (flash/paged/fused) taken from runtime annotations
- Host->device enqueue timestamps and device->host completion timestamps (latency per request)
- Per-token time series for a subset of traced requests (to see handoff points)
- Memory alloc/free and peak allocation per run
- Small counters: fusion-fallback-count, prefetch-missed-evict, kv-evict-wave
Tools and instrumentation notes:
- nvtx ranges injected at the runtime boundaries around: request dispatch, batch coalescer entry, fusion decision, kernel launch, kernel completion.
- Traces collected using nsight-systems with --trace=nvtx, --duration repeated and exported to json.
- Lightweight sampling profiler agent on the host to record queue lengths of the dispatcher every 500us.
- Modified runtime to add a "kernel-handshake-id" (monotonic per-request) passed through nvtx/annotations so we can correlate host logs to device kernels.
- Small library to stitch nsight json together with runtime logs (script in linked PR).
Key observations (initial):
1) Bimodal mix (C) at high KV-hit (95%) + fusion=on + flashpaged=enabled produced reproducible 99th spikes that coincide with a specific kernel handoff pattern: flash-attn kernel A -> tiny fused op shim -> fallback to unfused matmul due to register pressure. The nvtx trace shows a ~0.8–1.6ms stall between the fused shim exit and unfused matmul launch.
2) The stall correlates with a sudden rise in register spill events (seen in per-kernel PTX counters). The fused shim appears to change live register usage enough that the downstream unfused kernel's occupancy drops, causing the scheduler to wait for resource free.
3) Microburst trains increase the probability the runtime picks a non-optimal kernel variant (we observed an up to 3x increase in fusion-fallback-count) — likely because the batch coalescer chooses a fast-path to drain the burst which triggers a fusion path untested by steady-state sampling.
4) FlashPaged off vs on: enabling paged prefetch reduces average latency when long sequences dominate, but for mixed workloads it increases tail because prefetch eviction waves coincide with microbursts, forcing unexpected page loads inside FlashAttention that push it into a high register-use codepath.
5) Quantization: int8-qat runs showed fewer register-spill-induced fallbacks (lower occupancy overall) but increased cache thrashing in the kernel due to smaller working set alignment, leading to slightly worse 99th in several cells.
Analysis notes and emerging metrics:
- Fusion Instability Index (FII): percent of requests that experienced a fusion->fallback transition within their token sequence. This seems to be a better predictor of 99th latency than raw fusion-fallback-count.
- Handoff Entropy: Shannon-like metric over kernel-choice sequences per request. Higher entropy correlates with higher jitter.
- Eviction Wave Coherence: fraction of prefetch misses that occur within 2ms of a previous miss on the same allocation slab. High coherence correlates with larger tail spikes.
Actionable hypotheses and proposed mitigations:
H1: Make fusion decision more conservative when handoff entropy is high. Practical change: prefer stable unfused matmul for requests that have already seen a fused->fallback in the last N (configurable) requests on that worker.
H2: Add a microburst-aware coalescer mode that detects train arrivals and forces deterministic kernel variants (avoid fusing ephemeral batches).
H3: Improve flash-paged prefetch heuristics to avoid slab eviction during bursts — throttle prefetch when queue length spikes above threshold.
H4: Expose a sampling mode to run a fraction of requests with nvtx tracing in prod (1 in 10k) to collect live fusion-fallback telemetry without full trace overhead.
Open questions / unknowns:
- Are register spills the root cause, or just a symptom of misaligned shared memory usage? We need a deeper per-kernel SASS-level dump for selected runs.
- Can kernel layout be nudged via compiler flags to avoid the shim->fallback gap? (experiment candidate: force different blockSize/tiling on fused shim)
- How much of this is hardware-specific (we tested on A100 + H100); do older Ampere variants show same patterns?
- Cost vs benefit: more conservative fusion reduces avg throughput. Need a modeling run to quantify cost increase for a given 99th improvement.
Next experiments (planned):
- Controlled per-kernel SASS dump on two problematic runs (bimodal/high-KV) for A100 and H100; compare register allocation and shared memory footprints.
- Run microburst coalescer patch in canary with synthetic burst injection and compare FII and 99th.
- Add tiny delay between fused shim and subsequent kernel launch in controlled env to see if stall disappears (diagnostic only).
- Run longer (15m) to measure whether eviction-wave coherence persists over longer timescales or is only a warmup phenomenon.
Notes to reviewers:
- Raw nsight traces and stitched logs are attached in the linked PR. The script to produce FII and Handoff Entropy is under tools/profiling/mesh_trace.
- This doc is an experiment log — we expect parts to be rough. Primary ask: sanity-check the measurement assumptions (especially queue length sampling resolution) and flag any missing counters you think we should capture (e.g., l2_miss counters per-kernel).
- If you are reviewing empirically: focus on cells C @ KV=95% and microburst mode; that's where the most surprising behavior sits.

Appendix (quick command snippets):
- nvprof/nsight capture template: nsys profile --trace=nvtx,cuda --capture-range=nvtx --output=runX --stop-on-exit "--duration 120"
- runtime bootstrap for trace: RUNTIME_TRACE=1 TRACE_SAMPLING=500 ./serving-worker --config ...
- produce FII: python tools/profiling/mesh_trace/compute_fii.py --nsight runX.qdrep --log runX.log

Unresolved todo list (short):
- [ ] Run SASS dump on two kernels flagged in run-2025-02-18-03
- [ ] Add l2_miss and regspill sampling to runtime counters
- [ ] Prototype microburst-aware coalescer PR and benchmark (bench harness: bench/microburst-runner)
- [ ] Write short explainer for product about tradeoffs (2–3 slides)

End of log.
